The dispenser shall achieve a reduction in connection time of 20% versus a human operator as well as a connection success rate of 99% in a controlled environment and 95% or better in a real-world trial. Concepts and requirements were also developed for the automated fueling of commercial on-road vehicles with a target connection success rate of 95% using a modified off-the- shelf robot. Another objective was to improve the efficiency of automated fueling of heavy-duty vehicles with liquid hydrogen, specifically to increase the transfer efficiency of liquid hydrogen from tanker. While some loss of hydrogen is inevitable during these pressure transfer events, the aim of this research is to identify the optimum pressure and transfer rates depending on the fill level of supply and receiving tanks to minimize vented mass. To reliably and consistently meet these pressure and flow rate targets, we will determine which aspects of the transfer process can be automated using a control system to regulate valve open and close events. This work will leverage prior liquid hydrogen transfer modeling research funded internally at Plug to direct the design and execution of small- and full-scale experiments that will test our theoretical hypotheses. Process dynamics observed in the lower cost, small-scale system, are used to inform hardware requirements and process control points for the larger full-scale system. Page 6 of 31 7. Project Results and Discussion: 7.1 Demonstration of autonomous fueling of gaseous H for materials handling 2 Development of positioning accuracy of robotic fueling arm Testing was conducted to establish a baseline measurement of the accuracy and repeatability of a human operator positioning a lift truck in front of a dispenser. The goal was to establish the range of motion required for an autonomous fueling mechanism to mate a hydrogen nozzle with a receptacle on a fuel cell system installed in a forklift. The assumption is that the human operator is a worse case (less accurate, repeatable) than an AGV. This assumption will be tested in the next quarter by performing similar testing using an AGV. The testing was performed with several operators using all three classes of lift truck commonly used in distribution centers (Class 1 sit-down, Class 2 reach and Class 3 end- riders). For each type of truck, the operator was instructed to attempt to achieve an ideal position for fueling with the truck parallel to the dispenser at a fixed distance and lined up with the nozzle. A vision system consisting of a webcam and associated software reading AR (Augmented Reality) tags was used to measure this “home” position relative to the fixed guardrail surrounding the dispenser.
